newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Dresdner says euro costs less than expected.
newsitem.headline: Dresdner says euro costs less than expected.

text.p: Dresdner Bank AG, Germany's second largest commercial bank, said on Friday that it would likely spend less money on converting to Europe's common currency, the Euro, than it had initially planned.

Management board member Ernst-Moritz Lipp told Reuters that the costs to switch its systems to the euro in 1999 would likely total 150 million marks ($91.6 million) or less. This is less than the 200 million marks the bank had initially earmarked for the project.
Lipp said the bank would work towards the switchover, begun in 1995, and incur considerable financial and staff costs during that time.
On the other hand Lipp said re-programming computers at the end of the decade would likely be a more difficult adjustment as this involved all areas of the bank.
"We have noticed that the switchover of bank systems at the end of the decade will be more difficult than the adjustment to the Euro as it impacts all areas of the bank," Lipp said.
The bank needs to switch the first digits on various transactions which may be quite difficult as computers often have difficulties switching these two digits, Lipp explained.
